name: Skin rash in adults
summary: Most rashes are harmless and caused by irritation, allergy, eczema or a viral infection. A rash that does not fade under pressure or comes with feeling very unwell needs urgent help.

A rash with swelling of the lips, tongue or throat, or difficulty breathing
Skin that is blistering, peeling off in sheets or painful over large areas, especially after starting a new medicine
A rash with a stiff neck, sensitivity to light, confusion or extreme drowsiness
A rash with cold, blotchy or blue-tinged skin, fast breathing or feeling very unwell
urgentFlags: A rash with a high temperature
A rash that is spreading quickly
A painful rash on one side of the body or near the eye
A rash that is hot, swollen and painful
A new rash after starting a medicine

commonCauses.title: Contact dermatitis
commonCauses.detail: A red, itchy rash where the skin touched something irritating or that you are allergic to.

commonCauses.title: Eczema
commonCauses.detail: Dry, itchy, cracked patches that come and go.

commonCauses.title: Hives
commonCauses.detail: Raised, itchy welts that move around and fade within a day.

commonCauses.title: Viral infection
commonCauses.detail: Many viruses cause a widespread blotchy rash with mild illness.

commonCauses.title: Psoriasis or fungal infection
commonCauses.detail: Scaly patches, or a ring-shaped itchy rash.

selfCare: Avoid anything you think might be irritating your skin
Use a plain moisturiser (emollient) and mild, unperfumed soap
Cool compresses can soothe itching
Ask a pharmacist about antihistamines or mild steroid creams for itchy rashes
avoid: Scratching, which can cause infection
Hot baths and perfumed products
Strong steroid creams on the face or for long periods without advice

name: Itchy skin
summary: Itchy skin is very common and is often caused by dry skin, eczema or an allergy. It usually improves with moisturising and avoiding irritants.

urgentFlags: Itching with yellowing of the skin or the whites of the eyes
Itching all over during pregnancy, especially on the hands and feet

commonCauses.title: Dry skin
commonCauses.detail: Very common in older people and in cold weather.

commonCauses.title: Eczema or contact dermatitis
commonCauses.detail: Itchy, red, dry patches.

commonCauses.title: Allergic reaction or hives
commonCauses.detail: Itchy raised welts after contact with an allergen or medicine.

commonCauses.title: Scabies or lice

commonCauses.title: Underlying conditions

selfCare: Use a plain, unperfumed moisturiser (emollient) often
Take short, lukewarm baths or showers and pat skin dry
Wear loose cotton clothing
Ask a pharmacist about antihistamines or soothing creams

Perfumed soaps, bubble bath and hot water
Unproven 'detox' supplements

name: Hives

redFlags: Swelling of the lips, tongue, mouth or throat
Difficulty breathing, wheezing or a tight throat
Feeling faint, dizzy or collapsing
Hives with severe stomach pain or vomiting after a known allergen
urgentFlags: Hives with a high temperature and feeling unwell

Swelling around the eyes or lips without breathing problems

commonCauses.title: Allergic reaction

commonCauses.title: Viral infection
commonCauses.detail: Common in children, often with a cold.

commonCauses.title: Unknown cause

name: Acne and spots
summary: Acne is very common, especially in teenagers, and causes spots on the face, back and chest. Mild acne can be treated with pharmacy products, and effective treatments are available from a doctor.
redFlags: A spreading, hot, red, painful area of skin with a high temperature and feeling very unwell
urgentFlags: A painful, swollen, hot spot or lump that is spreading
Severe acne with fever and joint pain

commonCauses.title: Hormonal changes
commonCauses.detail: Puberty, periods, pregnancy and polycystic ovary syndrome increase oil production.

commonCauses.title: Blocked hair follicles
commonCauses.detail: Oil and dead skin block pores and bacteria cause inflammation.

commonCauses.title: Family history
commonCauses.detail: Acne often runs in families.

commonCauses.title: Cosmetics and medicines
commonCauses.detail: Oily make-up and some medicines can trigger spots.

selfCare: Wash affected areas twice a day with a mild cleanser and lukewarm water
Use non-comedogenic (non-pore-blocking) make-up and moisturisers
Ask a pharmacist about creams or gels containing benzoyl peroxide
Give treatments 2 to 3 months to work
avoid: Squeezing or picking spots, which can cause scarring
Washing more than twice a day or scrubbing hard
Unproven remedies such as toothpaste on spots
seeDoctorIf: Pharmacy treatments have not helped after 2 to 3 months
You have painful, deep spots or lumps (nodules or cysts)

Acne is affecting your confidence or mood

name: Hair loss
summary: Losing some hair every day is normal. Gradual thinning is often genetic, while sudden shedding can follow illness, stress or childbirth and usually grows back.
redFlags: Sudden hair loss with a severe rash, swelling of the face or difficulty breathing
urgentFlags: Hair loss with a painful, red, swollen or pus-filled scalp and a high temperature

commonCauses.title: Male or female pattern hair loss
commonCauses.detail: Gradual thinning that runs in families.

commonCauses.title: Telogen effluvium
commonCauses.detail: Shedding a few months after illness, stress, surgery, childbirth or weight loss; usually recovers.

commonCauses.title: Alopecia areata
commonCauses.detail: Round bald patches caused by the immune system.

commonCauses.title: Iron deficiency or thyroid problems
commonCauses.detail: Can cause diffuse thinning.

commonCauses.title: Hairstyles and treatments
commonCauses.detail: Tight braids, ponytails or harsh chemical treatments damage hair.

selfCare: Be gentle with your hair: use wide-toothed combs and avoid tight styles
Eat a balanced diet with enough protein and iron
Ask a pharmacist about over-the-counter treatments for pattern hair loss
avoid: Expensive 'miracle' hair-growth supplements and devices without evidence
Harsh chemical treatments and excessive heat styling
seeDoctorIf: You have sudden hair loss or bald patches

name: Itchy or flaky scalp
summary: An itchy, flaky scalp is usually caused by dandruff or seborrhoeic dermatitis and can be controlled with medicated shampoos. Head lice are another common cause, especially in children.

urgentFlags: A red, swollen, painful or pus-filled area on the scalp
A painful, blistering rash on one side of the head or forehead

commonCauses.title: Dandruff and seborrhoeic dermatitis

commonCauses.title: Head lice

commonCauses.title: Psoriasis or eczema

name: Nail changes
summary: Nail changes are common and are often caused by a fungal infection, injury or ageing. Some changes can be a sign of other health problems.
redFlags: Nails or fingertips that suddenly turn blue or grey, with difficulty breathing or feeling very unwell
urgentFlags: Red, hot, swollen skin around a nail that is spreading, with a high temperature
A painful, pus-filled swelling next to a nail

commonCauses.title: Fungal nail infection
commonCauses.detail: Thickened, discoloured, brittle nails, more often on toenails.

commonCauses.title: Injury
commonCauses.detail: Bruising under the nail or white marks after knocks.

commonCauses.title: Psoriasis or eczema
commonCauses.detail: Pitting, ridges or nails lifting from the nail bed.

commonCauses.title: Other health conditions

Wear well-fitting shoes and change socks daily
Ask a pharmacist about antifungal nail paints for mild fungal infections; treatment can take months

avoid: Sharing nail clippers or towels
Cutting cuticles or picking at nails

name: Ingrown toenail
summary: An ingrown toenail happens when the edge of the nail grows into the skin, usually on the big toe. It often improves with simple care, but infection needs treatment.
redFlags: Red, hot, swollen skin spreading up the foot or leg with a high temperature and feeling very unwell
urgentFlags: Pus, spreading redness or a high temperature
An ingrown toenail if you have diabetes or poor circulation

commonCauses.title: Cutting nails too short or curved

commonCauses.title: Tight shoes
commonCauses.detail: Pressure pushes the skin onto the nail.

commonCauses.title: Sweaty feet and nail shape
commonCauses.detail: Naturally curved nails are more prone to growing in.

Gently push the skin away from the nail with a cotton bud
Wear wide, comfortable shoes
Take paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain, following the pack instructions
Cut toenails straight across and not too short
avoid: Cutting the nail edge out yourself
Picking at the nail
Tight or pointed shoes

It keeps coming back

name: New lump under the skin
summary: Most lumps under the skin are harmless, such as cysts, fatty lumps or swollen glands. A new lump that does not go away, grows or feels hard should be checked by a doctor.
redFlags: A lump with rapidly spreading redness, severe pain and feeling very unwell or confused
A lump in the groin or tummy that is suddenly very painful and cannot be pushed back, with vomiting
urgentFlags: A lump that is red, hot, painful and swelling, especially with a high temperature
A lump in the neck with difficulty swallowing or breathing

commonCauses.title: Swollen glands
commonCauses.detail: Soft, tender lumps in the neck, armpit or groin during an infection; usually go down within 2 weeks.

commonCauses.title: Cysts
commonCauses.detail: Smooth, round lumps under the skin that may have a small dark spot in the middle.

commonCauses.title: Lipoma
commonCauses.detail: A soft, rubbery, movable fatty lump that grows slowly.

commonCauses.title: Abscess or boil
commonCauses.detail: A painful, red, swollen lump filled with pus.

commonCauses.title: Cancer
commonCauses.detail: Less commonly, a hard, painless lump that grows or does not move.

selfCare: Note the size, position and whether it is painful, and check it again over the following weeks
For a boil, hold a warm compress on it a few times a day
Make an appointment for any lump that worries you
avoid: Squeezing or trying to cut open a lump or boil
Ignoring a lump that is growing or hard
seeDoctorIf: A lump is bigger than about 2cm or getting bigger
A lump is hard and does not move
A lump has lasted more than 2 weeks
A lump comes back after removal

name: Changing or new mole
summary: Most moles are harmless, but a new mole or one that changes in size, shape or colour should be checked, as it can be an early sign of melanoma skin cancer.

urgentFlags: A mole that is growing quickly
A mole that has started bleeding, crusting or oozing

commonCauses.title: Normal mole changes
commonCauses.detail: Moles can change slowly over many years, especially in younger people and during pregnancy.

commonCauses.title: Seborrhoeic keratosis

commonCauses.title: Melanoma

Trying to remove a mole yourself, including with creams sold online

name: Bruising easily
summary: Bruising more easily is common with age and with some medicines. Unexplained bruising, especially with other symptoms, should be checked by a doctor.

Bruising with bleeding that will not stop
A bruise after a head injury with drowsiness, confusion or vomiting
Bruising with vomiting blood or black poo
urgentFlags: Lots of unexplained bruises or tiny red-purple spots appearing
Bruising with nosebleeds or bleeding gums
Bruising while taking blood thinners
Unexplained bruises on a child or a vulnerable adult

commonCauses.title: Ageing skin
commonCauses.detail: Skin and blood vessels become thinner, so bruises appear with minor knocks.

commonCauses.title: Medicines
commonCauses.detail: Blood thinners, aspirin, anti-inflammatory painkillers and long-term steroids increase bruising.

commonCauses.title: Unnoticed knocks
commonCauses.detail: Many bruises come from bumps you do not remember.

commonCauses.title: Blood or clotting disorders

Rest and raise the bruised area if you can
Make a list of all medicines and supplements you take to show the doctor
avoid: Stopping a prescribed blood thinner without talking to your doctor
Supplements that can affect bleeding, such as high-dose fish oil or ginkgo, without advice

urgentFlags: Eczema that is suddenly much worse, weeping, crusted or painful

Stopping a steroid cream suddenly or using strong ones for long periods without advice

Blisters in the mouth, eyes or genitals with a high temperature and feeling very unwell

Blisters from a burn that are larger than your hand
Blisters that keep appearing for no clear reason

commonCauses.detail: From shoes, tools or exercise.

commonCauses.title: Burns and sunburn

commonCauses.title: Skin conditions or infections

name: Insect bite or sting
summary: Most insect bites and stings cause a small, red, itchy lump that settles within a few days. Rarely, they can cause a serious allergic reaction or become infected.

Wheezing, difficulty breathing or a tight throat
Feeling faint, dizzy, confused or collapsing
A fast heartbeat with widespread hives or swelling
Being stung in the mouth or throat
urgentFlags: Redness and swelling spreading from the bite, or pus

A circular red rash spreading around a tick bite

commonCauses.detail: A red, itchy lump that may blister; common with mosquitoes, midges and fleas.

commonCauses.title: Large local reaction

commonCauses.title: Infection

Squeezing a tick's body or using heat, petroleum jelly or alcohol to remove it

You have been stung or bitten in the mouth, throat or near the eyes
You have had a bad reaction to a bite or sting before

A temperature of 40C (104F) or higher with hot skin that has stopped sweating
Fast breathing or breathlessness with feeling very unwell
urgentFlags: Large areas of blistering or swelling
Sunburn with a high temperature, chills, headache, dizziness or feeling sick

commonCauses.title: Not enough sun protection

commonCauses.title: Medicines

commonCauses.title: Contact dermatitis
commonCauses.detail: An itchy, blistering rash where the skin touched an irritant or plant.

commonCauses.title: Cold sores or impetigo
commonCauses.detail: Clusters of blisters, usually around the mouth or nose.

selfCare: Contact a doctor or pharmacist quickly, as early antiviral treatment can help
Take paracetamol for pain, following the pack instructions
Keep the rash clean and dry and wear loose clothing
Use a cool compress a few times a day
avoid: Contact with pregnant people who have not had chickenpox, newborn babies and people with weakened immune systems until the blisters have crusted over
Sharing towels
Covering the rash with plasters, which can slow healing
seeDoctorIf: Pain continues after the rash has healed
The rash is not crusting over after 10 days
You want to ask about the shingles vaccine

name: Cuts and grazes
summary: Most small cuts and grazes can be treated at home and heal within a few days. Deep cuts, heavy bleeding or signs of infection need medical attention.
redFlags: Bleeding that is heavy, spurting, or will not stop after 10 minutes of firm pressure
A deep wound to the chest, tummy, neck or head
An object stuck in the wound
Numbness, tingling or being unable to move the area beyond the cut
urgentFlags: A cut that is gaping, longer than about 5cm or that may need stitches
A cut from a human or animal bite
Dirt or debris that you cannot clean out
Signs of infection: increasing pain, swelling, redness, pus or a high temperature

commonCauses.title: Everyday accidents
commonCauses.detail: Knives, glass, falls and sports injuries.

commonCauses.title: Bites
commonCauses.detail: Human and animal bites carry a high risk of infection.

selfCare: Stop the bleeding by pressing firmly with a clean cloth and raising the area
Clean the wound under running tap water
Pat dry and cover with a plaster or sterile dressing
Take paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain, following the pack instructions
avoid: Using antiseptic on the wound, which can damage tissue; clean water is enough
Removing an object stuck deep in a wound
Picking at scabs
seeDoctorIf: A wound has not healed after 2 weeks
You are unsure if your tetanus vaccination is up to date and the wound is dirty
You have diabetes and a cut on your foot
